subject: Re: Performance SLO + Autoscale qualification — FastPay follow-up
messages:
From: Sam Price <sam.price@fastpay.com>

Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>

Subject: Performance SLO + Autoscale follow-up (FastPay)

Thanks again for the demo this morning — really helpful. Quick recap and a few clarifying items so we can align on next steps.

Summary of our targets / requirements:
- Latency: p95 < 300ms for ~256-token generations; p99 ideally < 750ms.
- Throughput: sustained ~120 req/s during business hours (peak windows ~1800–2000 PST).
- Concurrency: average concurrency ~150, peaks to 400 for short bursts.
- Streaming: we plan to use streaming responses for progressive UI; we need <100ms time-to-first-token for most calls.
- Autoscaling / burst: want ability to handle bursts up to 2.5x baseline for 2–5 minutes with minimal queuing.

Questions:
1) What scale-up times should we plan for from a cold pool vs a warm pool?
2) How do you surface queueing behavior (e.g., expected queued latency at 200% load)?
3) Can you quantify warm-pool sizing guidance (how many GPUs / instances to keep warm for our traffic shape)?

Attached is our internal SLO spreadsheet — includes hourly distribution by endpoint and average token lengths.

Next steps we propose:
- You confirm expected scale-up times and recommended warm-pool sizes for our traffic.
- Plan a short PoC (2–3 weeks) to validate scale behavior under our load profile.

If you can share a short mutual action plan and estimated PoC timeline, we can get procurement and infra on standby.
—Sam
Sam Price

sam.price@fastpay.com

Subject: Re: Performance SLO + Autoscale follow-up (FastPay)

Thanks Sam — great summary and helpful attachment. Looping in Mateo (capacity engineering) and Vivek (solutions) so they can provide the technical sizing and a proposed mutual action plan.

Quick answers up front:
- Cold start vs warm pool: cold-to-ready for a fully cold GPU worker is typically 45–75s depending on model size/quantization; with a configured warm pool we can get the effective scale-up (first-token) down to ~8–15s for new sessions.
- Queueing behavior: we provide request-level queueing metrics and an expected queued latency curve in our console; at sustained 200% of provisioned capacity you'll see increasing queued latency and token backpressure — we work with customers to set a target SLO and a buffer (warm pool + short queue) to keep p95 within target.
- Warm-pool guidance: for your profile (peaks to 400 concurrent, 120 sustained) we'd suggest a warm-pool sized to cover ~30–40% of peak concurrency initially (roughly 120–160 warm sessions) and autoscale rules to add capacity aggressively for short bursts (scale step + pre-warm).

Attached is a short note on our burst/warm-pool approach. Mateo, can you provide the PoC scope and proposed timeline (load window, canary stage, success criteria)? Vivek — any specific infra or security flags to note for procurement?

Proposed mutual action plan (high-level):
1) Share final SLO spreadsheet (Sam) — done.
2) Redwood to deliver PoC plan + resource estimate (Mateo) — by Tue 6/8.
3) FastPay to provision test accounts and sample traffic generator (Sam) — by Fri 6/11.
4) PoC run (2 weeks) with monitoring + joint review — target start Mon 6/14.

We’ll include a short document on warm-pool sizing and expected queued latency in the PoC pack.

Best,
Marissa Cole

marissa_cole@redwood.ai

From: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Performance SLO + Autoscale follow-up (FastPay)

Quick technical notes from capacity/infra side:
- Warm pools: we pre-allocate model worker contexts (KV cache warmed, kernels loaded). For the models we demoed, a warm context cuts cold-start overhead to ~8–12s to first-token.
- Pre-warm sizing: each warm context handles ~1 session-equivalent (concurrency depends on model and batching). For your 400-peak bursts we recommend starting with 120 warm contexts and an autoscale policy that steps capacity by 50% when queue depth exceeds 40% of provisioned concurrency.
- Burst strategy: use short, aggressive scale steps + staged pre-warm. For example: if queue depth > 40% for 30s -> add N warm contexts (N = 0.5 * provisioned), then monitor p95 and add another step if still over threshold. This keeps queued latency bounded for short bursts.
- Cold start fallback: for extremely large spikes beyond warm + autoscale, we surface a degraded-mode route (lower-cost model variant or higher-latency fallback) to avoid complete failures. That route typically has higher p95 but stays within functional SLOs.
- Observability: we’ll expose queue-depth, time-to-first-token, and worker-warmth metrics in the PoC dashboard.

PoC scope (proposed):
- Duration: 2 weeks (1-week ramp / 1-week soak).
- Targets: validate p95 < 300ms at 120 req/s sustained and maintain p95 < 750ms at 2.5x burst with <30s tails for queued requests.
- Tools: Redwood load harness + your traffic generator (we can run shared JMeter scenarios).
- Success criteria: p95 targets met during ramp and soak; automated scaling steps succeeded without >5% error spike.

I’ll draft the PoC plan doc and resource estimate and post by EOD Monday (6/7).
—Mateo
Mateo Alvarez
Capacity Engineering, Redwood Inference
